History · 24 November 2026

How the first intelligence test was born

Alfred Binet created it to help children who were falling behind at school. It was soon used for purposes he would not have approved of.

In 1904 France had just made schooling compulsory for all children. Teachers were faced with pupils who could not keep up with the class, and the government wanted an objective way to identify who needed adapted teaching. It gave the task to a commission that included the psychologist Alfred Binet.

Questions for each age

With his collaborator Théodore Simon, Binet put together in 1905 a series of tasks of increasing difficulty: following an object with the eyes, naming body parts, repeating digits, defining words, solving simple problems. The key idea was to compare each child with what children of the same age usually managed. This gave rise to the notion of mental age.

Binet's warnings

Binet insisted that his scale did not measure something fixed or innate, and that it was not meant to classify children once and for all. Its aim was to identify those who needed help so they could receive it. He criticised those who spoke of an unchangeable intelligence and proposed "mental orthopaedics" exercises to improve attention and memory.

What came next

Binet died in 1911. In the United States, Lewis Terman adapted the scale in 1916, called it the Stanford-Binet and popularised the intelligence quotient, an idea from the German William Stern. During the First World War tests were given to nearly two million recruits, and some of the results were used to justify laws restricting immigration and forced sterilisation programmes. The very opposite of what Binet had stood for.

Today intelligence tests are rigorous instruments, useful in clinical and educational assessment, but their history is a reminder of something important: a good tool can be misused when people forget what it was made for.

References

  1. Binet, A. y Simon, T. (1905). Méthodes nouvelles pour le diagnostic du niveau intellectuel des anormaux. L'Année psychologique, 11, 191–244.
  2. Nicolas, S., Andrieu, B., Croizet, J.-C., Sanitioso, R. B. y Burman, J. T. (2013). Sick? Or slow? On the origins of intelligence as a psychological object. Intelligence, 41(5), 699–711.
